In web development, a corporate website is often reduced to a set of pages, a CMS, and a frontend layer. But in scenarios where the first stages of supplier selection are carried out by AI agents, the site begins to play a more interesting role. It becomes not just an interface, but a node where identity, structured facts, claim provenance, and the action trail converge.

- The most important architectural principle here, in my view, is a single source of truth. Not a separate website for people and a separate API or agent layer maintained by hand, but a canonical business model from which both projections are rendered. This is standard engineering hygiene, but for some reason it is still rare in the commercial web. As soon as data on pricing, terms, and constraints starts to live in two places, the system becomes fragile and untrustworthy.
- The second principle is to distinguish between mere content and claims that carry risk or responsibility. An HTML page can display text about qualifications, a warranty, or provenance, but for a machine it still remains just text until there is a separate trust mechanism. From there, it becomes logical to think about signatures, domain binding, action logging, and the separation of the descriptive layer from verifiable evidence. Not as a fashionable feature, but as a natural evolution of web presence.
- The third point: baseline agent suitability seems to grow out of the old, familiar qualities of a well-built web. Semantic HTML, accessibility, stable structure, clean data, a reasonable approach to JS, and predictable rendering. In other words, "agent-ready" in the mature sense is not a new decorative layer, but a byproduct of correct architecture and publishing discipline.

If you had to define the minimum technical baseline for a website as a verifiable representation, what would you include in it first?
